item.title: China-chic keeps winning fans overseas
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
By Chen Zhuo, Zhao Zhilin BEIJING, Aug. 22 (Xinhuanet) -- A content creator recently shared a video on YouTube showcasing the souvenirs she brought home from a trip to China: a delicate hairpin, a panda pendant, several fridge magnets and a photo book featuring her dressed in Hanfu, a traditional style of Chinese clothing. Her collection offers a glimpse into the growing appeal of China-chic, a trend that is bringing Chinese aesthetics, traditional culture and contemporary creativity to consumers and audiences both at home and abroad. This photo collage features a content creator sharing Chinese souvenirs on her YouTube channel. (Screenshot from YouTube) From traditional Chinese clothing and intangible cultural heritage crafts to cultural and creative products and homegrown brands, the concept of China-chic has been increasingly visible in China's consumer markets and among international visitors. New Chinese-style outfit has emerged as one of the most recognizable expressions of the trend. Foreign visitors have tried on traditional Chinese clothing and taken part in Hanfu photography during their trips to China. For some, the experience has also led to purchases to take home and share on social media. The hashtag #Hanfu has been used in more than 350,000 posts on TikTok. Data from the General Administration of Customs show that China's goods trade reached 25.47 trillion yuan (about 3.75 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first half of 2026, up 16.9 percent year on year, with a growing number of culturally creative, technology-driven and brand-oriented consumer products entering overseas markets. South Korean tourists dressed in Hanfu, a traditional Chinese attire, pose for photos in Yuyuan Garden in Shanghai, east China, Jan. 6, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Haoming) Meanwhile, foreign travelers are increasingly moving beyond sightseeing. Immersive local experiences have become a popular way for them to understand China. According to a Xinhua think tank report titled "Shopping in China: Sharing New Opportunities of Open Development", international tourists are "completing their consumption through immersive participation" in activities such as Hanfu dressing, tea ceremony appreciation, calligraphy and painting. A foreign tourist learns about Xuan paper in Jingxian County, east China's Anhui Province, on June 20, 2026. (Photo by Li Xiaohong/Xinhua) Many overseas visitors are willing to participate in traditional craft activities, learn basic techniques, join folk celebrations and experience customs that have been preserved and adapted to contemporary life. Digital cultural tourism also brings fresh ways for international visitors to explore local traditions. Such experiences add more diverse elements into China-chic. Visitors are not only purchasing products with Chinese cultural elements but are engaging with the processes, stories and traditions behind them. A foreign tourist looks on as local women make Tiaohua cross-stitch embroidery, a traditional handicraft passed down through generations by women of Huayao, a branch of Yao ethnic group, at Huxingshan Yao Township in Longhui County, Shaoyang City, central China's Hunan Province, Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Zeng Yong/Xinhua) According to a report from iiMedia Research, the China-chic market is expected to surpass 3 trillion yuan (about 445 billion U.S. dollars) by 2028. China-chic has also been reflected in contemporary Chinese brands, whose products combine local cultural references with modern design, branding and consumer experiences. Croatian tourist Lori opens a "Labubu" blind box at Wangfujing shopping district in Beijing, capital of China, Feb. 6, 2026. (Xinhua/Song Yidai) Time-honored Chinese cultural symbols gain fresh global influence via social media. The vintage White Rabbit candy wrapper, for example, has gone viral overseas, as netizens reuse its rabbit motif on clothing and accessories. Trendy blind boxes from Pop Mart, alongside milk tea from local favorites like Chagee and Mixue Ice Cream & Tea, have become must-try items on inbound travel checklists. Tourists from Russia select cultural and creative products at a bookstore in Jiangbei District of Ningbo City, east China's Zhejiang province, July 28, 2026. (Xinhua/Jiang Han) For overseas visitors, China-chic may begin with something as simple as a souvenir from a trip, but it can linger as a memory of what they made, wore, watched or experienced. As traditional crafts, Chinese aesthetics and contemporary brands reach more consumers overseas, China-chic is becoming a channel through which people encounter and experience Chinese culture.

item.title: U.S., Canada fail to reach trade deal
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
WASHINGTON/OTTAWA, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- The United States and Canada failed to reach a trade deal on Friday, and the White House said that it would impose 50 percent tariffs on certain imports from Canada. Meanwhile, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada would retaliate on the new tariffs. Carney said Canada has suspended trade negotiations with the United States and recalled its negotiators to Ottawa, following new tariff threats from Washington. The decision was made after last-minute changes proposed by the U.S. side were deemed "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," he said in a statement. As the U.S. intends to impose a 50-percent tariff on 20 billion U.S. dollars worth of Canadian goods starting midnight, Canada will match those tariffs "dollar for dollar" to protect its workers and businesses, Carney said. ■

item.title: Chinese commercial space firm completes long-duration test of reusable rocket engine
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- China's commercial reusable launch vehicle sector continues to make steady progress, as a company announced on Friday that it had completed a long-duration test firing of an engine for a large recoverable carrier rocket. Deep Blue Aerospace, a commercial space startup based in Wuxi, east China's Jiangsu Province, said it recently completed a 100-second static-fire test of its Thunder-RS engine, a 130-tonne-class liquid-oxygen kerosene engine designed for the company's large reusable rocket, Nebula-2. The test reached 1,297.5 kilonewtons of thrust, or about 132.3 tonnes. The company said multiple short-duration test firings had been conducted previously to evaluate engine performance, with no anomalies recorded. The recent 100‑second run was the engine's first crossing of that steady‑state duration threshold, serving as a comprehensive verification of its performance, the company said. Rocket reusability can greatly cut launch costs and boosts launch frequency, making it key to achieving large-scale, routine access to space. China launched the reusable rocket Zhuque-3 on Wednesday morning, achieving its first recovery of a rocket's first stage on land, marking the country's first successful land-based recovery. This mission followed the successful sea-based net recovery of the Long March-10B's first stage on July 10. More models of Chinese reusable rockets are scheduled to conduct tests this year. ■

item.title: Chinese cities promote greener "central cooling" to beat heat
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
* Wuhan is tapping water from the Yangtze River to cool buildings while reducing energy use and carbon emissions. * Chinese cities are exploring lower-carbon cooling solutions based on local conditions and resources. * Extreme heat is posing a growing challenge worldwide, highlighting the need for more sustainable cooling. WUHAN, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- As the summer sun blazes over Wuhan, a city in central China known for its intense heat, gym operator Wu Jing has found an unlikely source of cooling: the Yangtze River. Wu used to spend about 15,000 yuan (about 2,212 U.S. dollars) a month on electricity to cool his 1,200-square-meter fitness club. The bill fell to about 10,000 yuan last month after the gym switched from conventional air conditioning to a centralized river-water cooling system. Wu said the new system also keeps temperatures more consistent throughout the gym, so club members don't have to deal with sudden changes when moving to the stretching area after working up a sweat. The gym is among several buildings cooled by a river-water energy station that began trial operations this summer. As a government-backed low-carbon demonstration project, the station currently supplies cooling to about 260,000 square meters of building space, including a primary school and a commercial complex, and is eventually expected to cover more than 2.1 million square meters. Water is drawn from about five meters above the bed of the Yangtze, China's longest river. At that depth, the water temperature ranges from 23 to 29 degrees Celsius, well below summer air temperatures, which can exceed 35 degrees Celsius, said Xiao Haixi, executive deputy general manager of the project company. After filtration, heat pumps use the temperature difference to cool buildings in summer and heat them in winter before returning the water to the Yangtze. According to Xiao, the system uses the river water only for heat exchange and does not consume it, and river water, water circulating inside the energy station and water used in buildings are kept in three separate systems. The water volume drawn from and returned to the Yangtze amounts to less than 0.01 percent of the river's flow, thus the water's temperature fluctuates only slightly after heat exchange, said Xiao. "The ecological impact is therefore limited and meets relevant standards." Once fully operational, the project is expected to save 7,374 tonnes of standard coal and cut carbon dioxide emissions by 18,000 tonnes annually -- equivalent to planting 1.05 million trees, Xiao added. The main structure of a 30,000-cubic-meter energy storage pool has also been completed. It will use cheaper off-peak electricity at night to store cooling or heating energy for use during the day, further lowering operating costs. GREENER ALTERNATIVES TO AIR CONDITIONERS Unlike central heating using hot water, which is widely used across northern China, centralized cooling using chilled water remains a niche solution in the country -- largely limited to office buildings and commercial complexes. Fu Lin, a professor at Tsinghua University's School of Architecture, wrote in China Science Daily that central cooling has been explored in China for over two decades, yet its adoption has been hampered by challenges including difficult access to cooling sources and high distribution costs. Nevertheless, Fu sees potential in combining central cooling with seasonal cold storage, including using surplus electricity in winter and spring to make ice and storing the resulting cooling energy for summer use. The existing networks of heating pipelines can also be utilized to distribute cooling. Such new cooling systems have been launched in several Chinese cities. In Xuzhou, east China's Jiangsu Province, the country's first residential central cooling project using water from an abandoned coal mine began operations in July. It cuts energy consumption by about half compared with conventional air conditioning, according to the project operator. In Jinan, capital of east China's Shandong Province, an energy station 21 meters underground provides centralized cooling to about 1 million square meters of building space. Chilled water is delivered through an underground pipe network that is also used for heating in winter. The station's centrifugal water chillers used for producing chilled water boast significantly higher efficiency than conventional split air conditioners, while also substantially reducing the use of refrigerants that contribute to global warming. These low-carbon cooling projects align well with China's commitment to achieving its dual carbon goals -- peaking carbon dioxide emissions before 2030, and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060. According to a national climate change plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China aims to reduce carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP by 17 percent by 2030 from 2025 levels. But not all green solutions to summer heat require complex cooling systems. In Wuhan and Chongqing, civil-defense facilities such as air-raid shelters have been opened as public cooling spaces in summer. In Wuhan alone, five such shelters can provide cooling to more than 9,000 people a day. Above ground, many Chinese cities have built a constellation of pocket parks, many of which are small and previously underused urban spaces. Statistics suggest that more than 18,000 such parks were built across China between 2021 and 2025 to help cities cushion against the heat island effect. Extreme heat poses a growing challenge worldwide. The World Meteorological Organization said this July was the world's second warmest July on record, with extreme heat, persistent drought and wildfires affecting large parts of the Northern Hemisphere. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has called extreme heat a "society-wide threat" and urged countries to expand access to sustainable cooling. Chen Yanhua, a senior engineer with CITIC General Institute of Architectural Design and Research Co., Ltd., said the growing use of river water, mine water, green spaces and other locally available resources reflects a broader shift in how Chinese cities respond to extreme heat. It marks a shift away from heavy reliance on energy-intensive air conditioning toward greater use of natural cooling sources and green infrastructure, which is more environmentally friendly and sustainable, said Chen. "These measures bring tangible benefits to residents," he added. ■ (Reporting by Cheng Lu, Yue Wenwan, Yao Yuan, Gong Liankang and Bai Xu; Video reporters: Xiong Xianghe; Video editors: Zhang Yueyuan, Roger Lott, Zheng Qingbin and Zhang Ning.)

item.title: Rocket launches fuel industrial tourism boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- For some, watching a rocket soar into the sky has made their space dreams feel closer than ever. Chi Xingyu, a middle school student from Shanghai, is one such dreamer. "I used to think rockets were far away from ordinary people. I never imagined I could stand on a beach and watch a launch with my own eyes," said Chi. Once a distant spectacle reserved for a few, rocket launches are emerging as a tourist draw in China, from Haiyang City in east China's Shandong Province to Wenchang City in China's southernmost island province of Hainan. The appeal lies in the immersive experience. Many visitors say that watching a launch on a screen can't compare to seeing it in person, where each site offers its own unique atmosphere shaped by the local landscape. "In Wenchang, you can see rockets soaring above coconut groves, while in northwest China's Jiuquan, you can witness a rocket rising from the desert," said Wei Ninghao, a 14-year-old space enthusiast. Yet, the "rocket-chasing" tourism is about much more than the brief, awe-inspiring launch. Local authorities are working to convert one-time visitors into repeat tourists by extending the aerospace experience. Hours before the launch, the viewing area in Haiyang was already buzzing with activities. Performances rolled out one after another. Robot dogs wove through the crowd, drawing children to chase, laugh and pose for photos. Space-themed merchandise was sold alongside Haiyang's local intangible cultural heritage crafts. In Haiyang, home to China's only commercial offshore launch port, tourists can tour rocket assembly plants and even board launch vessels. At the local aerospace science museum, visitors explore space engineering through VR, AR, and interactive, hands-on exhibits. "We have developed regular study tour programs tailored for students of different ages, helping visitors truly understand aerospace, instead of merely watching rockets," said Sun Yuqian of the Oriental Maritime Spaceport (Shandong) Development Group Co., Ltd. The museum receives about 100,000 visitors annually, and rocket launch viewing has attracted over 200,000 tourists so far. The economic ripple effects go far beyond the excitement of the launch itself. "During launches, nearby hotels are fully booked, and my restaurant's revenue doubles compared to normal days," said Li Ying, a local restaurateur. In Wenchang, the strategy is to integrate aerospace with local advantages, such as visits to coconut groves and beachcombing, to extend tourists' stays. "Now that viewing a launch is a regular occurrence, we are willing to spend more time planning trips and buying local goods," said Guo Chenchen, a tourist from central China's Henan Province. Experts said that this tourism boom is underpinned by solid industrial strength rather than mere novelty. In Haiyang, for instance, a six-kilometer Space Avenue links rocket manufacturing, satellite development, and offshore launch facilities, allowing visitors to get up close to the nation's space infrastructure. "Rocket launches possess strong visual appeal and educational value, making them a natural fit for tourism," said Liu Jia, a professor at the College of Management of Ocean University of China. "What was once a niche pursuit by enthusiasts has evolved into a new consumption scenario for families and study-tour groups." This surge in "rocket-chasing" tourism is part of a larger boom in industrial tourism across China. Observers note that the trend reflects rising public interest in science and technology. Topics like AI, smart manufacturing, aerospace, and new energy are drawing more attention, sparking curiosity among parents and students alike. Liu said that family travel spending is shifting from mere sightseeing to knowledge-driven, experience-based consumption, with parents more willing to pay for products that combine fun with learning. Authorities are ramping up policy support. For instance, the country released a new five-year tourism development plan this year to further develop industrial tourism, including encouraging enterprises to showcase their achievements in aerospace, shipbuilding and other manufacturing sectors. ■

item.title: China Focus: China embraces summer inbound travel craze with niche draws, fresh moves
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- At more than 1,500 meters above sea level, Tianmen Mountain in central China's Zhangjiajie offers summer temperatures of just 22 to 26 degrees Celsius, drawing a steady stream of visitors. Among them are growing numbers of European travelers, like Italian Giancarlo Marino. Escaping the relentless summer heat in his hometown, he traveled to China with friends in search of cooler weather. "Here you can feel the breeze, and while you're resting up on the mountain, you can even buy ice-cold drinks from the many vendors. It's thoughtful and relaxing," he said. As extremely high temperatures grip many parts of the world this summer, China is emerging as an unexpected destination to avoid the soaring temperatures. With more convenient entry policies and a host of tourism-friendly measures, the country is drawing international visitors in surprising new ways. NICHE ATTRACTIONS Jizhou District in north China's Tianjin Municipality is usually known among Beijing residents as a weekend escape. Few would expect to encounter overseas tourists there, let alone visitors from Argentina. Argentine traveler Michael visited Jizhou during his trip to China to enjoy the mountain scenery around the Huangyaguan section of the Great Wall. For him, the "coolness" of Jizhou was not just about the pleasant temperature, but also about immersing himself in nature and experiencing rural life. "The environment here is beautiful, and you can even see the Great Wall from the guesthouse," he said. Local guesthouse owner Zhang Wei has noticed a growing number of foreign visitors seeking a deeper understanding of local life instead of simply checking off famous attractions. "We've lately seen a clear increase in overseas guests. Many like to combine countryside experiences with natural scenery, allowing them to experience China in a more in-depth way," Zhang said. Dutch tourist Noa is another traveler seeking out niche experiences. On a recent independent trip to Nanjing in east China's Jiangsu Province, Noa and friends made a point of visiting local produce markets and public parks, including matchmaking corners where parents gather to find partners for their children, to observe daily life up close. "Many of the vegetables here are things I've never seen back home. It's really interesting," Noa said. China's rapid economic and social development is also reshaping inbound tourism. Slovenian tourist Rainer Grega, visiting China for the first time, said he hopes to tour major Chinese technology companies. "Many Chinese companies and brands are well-known overseas, so I'm really looking forward to visiting the headquarters of some of them. It would be fascinating to tour an electric-vehicle factory or see how those advanced robots are manufactured," he said. According to a representative of a Suzhou-based international travel agency, foreign visitors are increasingly planning multi-city itineraries, while younger independent travelers, trips to smaller cities and rural areas, and longer stays have all become notable trends. "Nowadays, many foreign visitors venture into city neighborhoods and rural villages to experience authentic Chinese life. From vibrant urban nightlife to rural revitalization, a vivid, multi-dimensional China is being increasingly shared with the world," said Wu Guoping, president of the Wuxi Tourism Association. MORE OPEN STANCE For many overseas visitors, China's increasingly convenient entry policies have provided an important guarantee for more flexible and in-depth travel. China currently offers unilateral visa-free entry to nationals of 50 countries, including Slovenia and Italy. "Thanks to the 30-day visa-free policy, you can come whenever you want -- just book a flight and go," Grega said. He added that transfers between airports and high-speed rail stations were seamless, making detailed travel planning largely unnecessary. Marino echoed the view, saying the visa-free policy was a major reason for choosing China. "It feels like the policy is becoming more and more foreigner-friendly. You can tell that China is opening its arms and genuinely welcoming more people to visit and learn about the country," he said. Data from the National Immigration Administration (NIA) showed that China recorded 22.91 million inbound foreign visits in the first half of this year, up 20.4 percent year on year. Of those, 77.7 percent were made under visa-free entry facilitation policies. China is also expanding the coverage of its 240-hour visa-free transit policy. According to an NIA announcement released on Aug. 20, citizens of Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam became eligible for the 240-hour visa-free transit policy and the 30-day visa-free entry policy for Hainan Province starting Aug. 20. The move increased the number of countries covered by the 240-hour visa-free transit policy to 57. Vietnamese student Do Thi Huyen My, now in her second year at Hainan University, happily welcomed the new policy. "I think the policy will definitely attract more Vietnamese tourists to China, especially to Hainan," she said. "For me personally, it also means my family can visit me in Hainan more conveniently while enjoying a vacation here. By the time I graduate, my parents, relatives and friends will also be able to attend my graduation ceremony without going through complicated visa procedures," My said. REFINED SERVICES MATTER As inbound visitors become increasingly diverse and venture beyond traditional destinations, new opportunities have emerged for China's tourism industry, alongside higher expectations for service quality. The city of Suzhou in Jiangsu Province, for instance, recently introduced a package of incentive measures to boost inbound tourism, offering rewards to travel agencies and online travel platforms that manage to organize overnight stays for foreign tourists and expatriates, or arrange one-day tours, with the annual reward up to 3 million yuan (about 442,000 U.S. dollars). Senior tour guides who manage to cultivate or recruit foreign-language guides are also eligible for incentives. However, experts warned that feedback from some foreign visitors suggests that information access and language services remain weak links amid the boom of inbound tourism, which underscores the need to improve tourism services for international guests. Wu Guoping suggested building a more comprehensive support system by developing multilingual digital platforms that seamlessly connect transportation, accommodation, dining, shopping and attractions, making travel planning and consumption more convenient. To that end, Shanghai has recently launched a type of integrated smart tourism service kiosk that combines abundant online and offline resources. Resembling a telephone booth, the facility provides access to 14,000 ticketing and shopping links, more than 20,000 dining venues and over 7,500 hotels and guesthouses. Powered by an AI travel assistant, it offers personalized recommendations, real-time interpretation and AI-generated travel journals. Its foreign bank card payment system supports 10 languages and more than 120 currencies. Zhangjiajie is also improving services to match its surging international guests. From January to July this year, the city received 860,700 inbound visitors from 195 countries and regions, up 19.01 percent year on year. Tourism foreign exchange revenue reached 98.52 million U.S. dollars, an increase of 40.52 percent. Despite the rapid growth, a previous survey in the Wulingyuan Scenic Area found that fewer than one-third of frontline staff could communicate proficiently in a foreign language. The scenic area has since partnered with local universities to compile English-, Korean- and other foreign-language learning handbooks, while organizing evening classes for tourism workers. Chen Heng, a 52-year-old publicity officer and one of the evening school participants, has even purchased language-learning software at his own expense and practices English pronunciation by reading aloud with a chopstick in his mouth. "Zhangjiajie boasts world-class natural scenery. Our service quality has to keep pace as well," he said. ■

item.title: China solicits public opinions on revised draft of administrative measures for outbound investment
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- China's National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) has released a revised draft of the administrative measures for outbound investment for public comment, aiming to better balance development and security in outbound investment. The draft updates the 2017 administrative measures for outbound investment by enterprises in response to rapid growth and significant changes in the external environment. The new measures further affirm the principal role of various investors. They also introduce reporting systems for major adverse events, large overseas reinvestment projects, and project completion status, aiming to better protect outbound investment rights and interests and help investors guard against overseas risks. The NDRC will further improve the draft based on public feedback and draft supporting documents and FAQs in order to better safeguard the balancing of development and security in outbound investment at the institutional level, according to the commission. China's outbound direct investment across all industries reached 596.42 billion yuan (about 86.53 billion U.S. dollars) during the first six months of 2026, representing an increase of 3.8 percent year on year, official data showed. China's domestic investors engaged in non-financial direct investment in 6,867 overseas companies across 144 countries and regions, with the investment value totaling 453.06 billion yuan, according to data released by the Ministry of Commerce and the State Administration of Foreign Exchange. China should expand the space for mutually beneficial international economic and trade cooperation, according to a July 30 meeting of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee. The meeting emphasized the need to improve the management system for outbound investment and strengthen comprehensive overseas service systems, while continuing efforts to actively attract and utilize foreign investment. ■

item.title: Xi congratulates Hichilema on re-election as Zambian president
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday congratulated Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election as president of Zambia. In his message, Xi said that they have met twice in recent years, and jointly steered the development of China-Zambia relations. The political mutual trust between the two countries has continued to deepen, practical cooperation has been fruitful, and China and Zambia have closely coordinated and cooperated in multilateral affairs, he said. Xi said he attaches great importance to the development of China-Zambia ties, and stands ready to work with Hichilema to implement the outcomes of the Beijing Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation. He also pledged to join the Zambian leader in carrying forward traditional friendship, cementing mutual support, and continuously raising the level of mutually beneficial cooperation, so as to take the China-Zambia comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership to new heights and deliver greater benefits to the two peoples. ■
